note: Calibration ledger: one falsifiable claim per side per edition, with a plain-English resolution condition and check-back date. Status: open | vindicated | falsified | unresolvable.

claims.claim: Consumer AI and work/agentic AI are diverging into effectively separate technologies, and the agentic-work side is where the durable economic value lands.
claims.resolution: By the check date, the bulk of frontier-lab revenue growth is attributable to API/agentic and enterprise usage rather than consumer subscriptions, and commentary has normalised treating 'consumer AI' and 'work AI' as distinct categories. Fails if consumer subscriptions remain the dominant revenue engine and the framing collapses back to a single 'AI'.

claims.claim: AI has no measurable ROI; firms cannot reliably measure either the benefit or the per-task cost, so spend will prove unjustifiable once examined.
claims.resolution: By the check date, no widely accepted standard for measuring AI ROI or per-task cost has emerged and at least one further large enterprise publicly caps or cuts AI spend citing unmeasurable return. Fails if credible, audited enterprise ROI measurement becomes routine and spend grows on the back of it.

claims.claim: Fable 5 is a genuine capability step change in agentic coding, not a saturated-benchmark illusion, and will translate into materially larger real-world tasks being handed to agents.
claims.resolution: By the check date, multiple independent enterprises report production agentic-coding workflows running many hours unattended and shipping merged code at scale (in the spirit of the Stripe 50M-line migration). Fails if Fable-class gains prove demo-bound and day-to-day developer workflows look essentially unchanged.

claims.claim: AI progress is slowing, and capability gains will not close the gap to the ~$2 trillion/yr in revenue the infrastructure build-out requires by 2030.
claims.resolution: By the check date, frontier-lab and hyperscaler AI revenue run-rate is tracking well below the trajectory needed to reach ~$2T/yr by 2030 while capex keeps rising. Fails if AI revenue growth visibly accelerates onto that trajectory.

claims.claim: Anthropic holds durable, structural gatekeeping power over frontier access: it will keep setting terms (guardrails, access tiers) that customers and competitors must accept.
claims.resolution: By the check date, Anthropic is still imposing access/usage terms that enterprise customers broadly accept without forcing reversal, and retains its enterprise position despite the Fable 5 backlash. Fails if competitive/price pressure forces Anthropic to materially open access or it loses significant enterprise share over trust.

claims.claim: Anthropic's apparent strength is borrowed: its profitability is an accounting artefact resting on subsidised compute, and its costs still scale linearly with revenue.
claims.resolution: When Anthropic discloses audited financials (e.g. via an IPO prospectus), they show costs scaling with revenue and no durable operating-margin path, with any prior 'profit' tied to one-off discounted-compute timing. Fails if audited figures show a credible, structural path to profitability.

claims.claim: Total token consumption growth will dwarf any revenue lost to enterprises shifting to cheaper token baskets.
claims.resolution: By the check date, OpenAI + Anthropic combined revenue run-rate is at least 30% above the ~$60B/yr projected for 2026, without across-the-board price rises doing the work.

claims.claim: AI revenue growth is slowing and will slow further as token-based billing exposes true costs to customers.
claims.resolution: By the check date, labs' quarter-on-quarter revenue growth has visibly flattened versus 2025, or a second wave of enterprise spending caps arrives at lower limits than Uber's $1,500/seat.

claims.claim: The Fable shutdown is a durable turning point: government will be materially more involved in gating frontier-model deployment, and access controls (KYC/citizenship checks) will spread rather than revert.
claims.resolution: By the check date, at least one of: a second US government-ordered restriction, recall, or forced disablement of a frontier model; OR formal citizenship/ID verification gating access to a frontier model on at least one major platform (Claude, Cursor, OpenRouter, etc.). If neither occurs and the directive is quietly reversed with no lasting controls, the claim fails.

claims.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic have no path to profitability; their IPO filings are a race for exit liquidity rather than evidence of viable economics.
claims.resolution: When OpenAI or Anthropic discloses audited financials via an IPO prospectus, the figures show continued large net losses with no credible near-term operating-margin path. If either company discloses profitability or a clear, dated path to it, the claim fails.

claims.claim: The Fable standoff is interpersonal, not technical: it will only be resolved by direct principal-level engagement (Amodei with senior administration figures), not by an engineering fix.
claims.resolution: When Fable/Mythos access is restored, contemporaneous reporting attributes the resolution chiefly to direct executive/political engagement (e.g. Amodei meeting administration principals) rather than to a technical remediation of the jailbreak. Fails if access returns via a documented technical fix with no such engagement, or via litigation alone.

claims.claim: OpenAI has no path to profitability and its losses are compounding, not narrowing (reported up ~8x in 2025 on ~$34B of spending).
claims.resolution: OpenAI's audited financials (via IPO prospectus or comparable disclosure) show 2025 net loss materially larger than 2024 and no credible near-term operating-margin path. Fails if OpenAI discloses profitability or a clear, dated path to it.

claims.claim: Over the next 6-12 months the labs will dramatically increase investment in enablement, training and expanding usage depth — even labs that don't believe everyone should build agents will act as if it's true, to hit quarterly token-growth targets.
claims.resolution: By the check date, major labs (Anthropic and/or OpenAI) have materially expanded enablement/training programmes, customer-success/forward-deployed capacity or usage-depth initiatives. Fails if no such material expansion in lab-led training/enablement is observable.

claims.claim: Token-based billing is fundamentally unprofitable and has triggered a customer revolt; 'training people to burn more tokens' is demand-manufacture that won't fix the missing ROI, and enterprise token budgets will keep being capped.
claims.resolution: By the check date, enterprise token-spend caps persist or spread and there is no credible evidence that lab enablement/training converted into measurable ROI sufficient to lift those budgets. Fails if enablement demonstrably lifts capped budgets with attributable value.

claims.claim: OpenAI's 2025 loss is largely a one-time non-cash accounting charge ($41.55bn from the for-profit conversion), and the underlying inference business is already profitable — $13.07bn revenue on $7.5bn cost of revenue — so the company is far healthier than the $38.5bn headline loss implies.
claims.resolution: A future audited disclosure or IPO prospectus shows that, with the one-time fair-value/conversion charge excluded, OpenAI's operating loss narrows year-over-year and inference/gross profit scales. Fails if operating losses (ex one-time items) keep widening with no margin path.

claims.claim: OpenAI's losses are mounting dramatically year over year (operating loss of $20.92bn in 2025 on $34bn of spending) with no visible path to sustainability or profitability.
claims.resolution: OpenAI's next audited figures show its operating loss (excluding one-time conversion charges) larger than 2025 with no credible near-term operating-margin path. Fails if OpenAI discloses a narrowing operating loss or a clear dated path to operating profitability.

claims.claim: Open-weight and routed model stacks (e.g. GLM 5.2, OpenRouter Fusion, compound APIs) can deliver near-Fable/near-frontier performance on real enterprise tasks at a fraction of the cost — around 6¢ vs 49¢ per task in the landing-page example — making smart routing and inference optimisation a durable competitive advantage.
claims.resolution: Within 12 months, independent benchmarks or large enterprises report production workloads moved to open-weight/routed stacks at materially lower cost with quality within a few points of frontier models. Fails if open/routed stacks consistently underperform on real tasks (as the Kimi K2.7 benchmark-vs-reality gap warns) and enterprises revert to frontier models.

claims.claim: The shift to cheaper models reflects the bursting of an AI 'tokenomics bubble' — enterprises put on usage-based billing in early 2026 revolted at the true cost, forcing providers into 'drastic' price cuts; most users will refuse to pay AI's actual cost, so the economics still don't work.
claims.resolution: Within 12 months, major AI providers report shrinking enterprise spend/renewals or further forced price cuts amid persistent operating losses on inference. Fails if enterprise AI spend and renewals grow while providers move inference to sustainable gross margins.

claims.claim: Companies that build a model-agnostic learning loop on top of AI — captured workflows, private evals measuring real business outcomes, RL environments trained on internal traces — will own durable, portable IP (token capital) that survives any single model swap, while those that merely pick a model cede their value to the model providers.
claims.resolution: Within 18 months, case studies or audited results show firms that built such owned learning systems demonstrating durable, portable productivity or ROI gains (net of token costs) that persist across a model change and differentiate them from peers who just bought a model. Fails if no measurable, portable advantage from 'token capital' systems emerges and outcomes track model choice and spend rather than owned scaffolding.

claims.claim: Enterprise AI has no measurable ROI and is not getting cheaper: there is no standard way to measure the cost of a task, AI remains more expensive than three years ago, and enterprises moved to token-based billing in 2026 will keep capping or cutting spend rather than finding sustainable returns.
claims.resolution: Within 12 months, enterprises continue to report spend caps/cuts and there is still no industry-standard measure of AI cost-per-task or ROI, while real (unsubsidised) inference cost has not durably fallen. Fails if a credible standard ROI measure emerges and enterprise AI spend grows on sustainable inference margins.

claims.claim: GLM 5.2 marks a durable break from the two-horse race: unlike previous Chinese open-weight models that benchmarked well then faded within weeks, capable open and runner-up models will now hold real, sustained production usage, so within 18 months a meaningful and growing share of organisations run non-frontier-lab models for genuine workloads rather than only as experiments.
claims.resolution: By end 2027, usage/adoption data show open-weight or runner-up models holding a material, non-trivial and growing share of enterprise AI production workloads, with GLM 5.2-class models still in real use rather than abandoned. Fails if GLM 5.2 and peers fade from real usage within months (as prior Chinese releases did) and production stays dominated by OpenAI and Anthropic.

claims.claim: AI capability and revenue growth are slowing just as the economics need them to accelerate: there is essentially no profitable paying AI demand outside OpenAI and Anthropic (and their hyperscaler backers), and enterprises will keep capping token spend rather than expanding it, so no large new base of sustainable AI compute demand will emerge.
claims.resolution: Within 12 months, enterprise token-spend caps persist or spread and no credible profitable base of AI compute demand emerges outside the two big labs and hyperscalers. Fails if a sizeable, profitable source of AI demand outside OpenAI/Anthropic appears with enterprise AI spend growing on sustainable margins rather than being capped.

claims.claim: The scary water and electricity figures driving data-centre opposition do not survive context, and the productive path is negotiated community benefit: as projects mature, more communities hosting large AI data centres will secure concrete, documented economic concessions (tax-funded local benefits, ratepayer protections, jobs) of the kind seen in Richland Parish, Louisiana, rather than either blocking projects or getting nothing.
claims.resolution: By end 2027, multiple US data-centre host communities have publicly documented negotiated benefits (e.g. ratepayer-protection commitments, cost-causation rules like Oregon's POWER Act, or tax-funded local payouts), and credible analyses continue to show data-centre water/electricity impacts are modest in context. Fails if host communities mostly absorb costs without concessions, or data-centre water/power demand proves a materially larger local burden than the edition claims.

claims.claim: The headline AI data-centre build-out is substantially overstated: claimed gigawatt-scale capacity is mostly phased, partly-built or mislabelled as 'operational', no true one-gigawatt facility has actually been completed and switched on, and hyperscalers will continue to avoid disclosing genuine completed operational capacity.
claims.resolution: By end 2026, independent verification of fully completed and operational AI data-centre capacity still falls well short of headline gigawatt figures, and hyperscalers still do not disclose audited completed capacity. Fails if a genuine one-gigawatt-plus facility is verifiably completed and fully operational, or hyperscalers publish audited operational-capacity figures matching the headline build-out.

claims.claim: Claude Tag-style persistent, in-workspace AI teammates represent a durable shift from prompting to delegation that becomes an organisational dependency: within roughly eighteen months a substantial share of knowledge organisations will run persistent in-workspace AI agents (in Slack, Teams or similar) as a standard, relied-upon part of normal workflow, not just pilots.
claims.resolution: By end 2027, persistent in-workspace AI teammates are in mainstream enterprise use with documented, repeated workflow reliance and productivity, beyond experiments at AI-native firms. Fails if such agents remain niche, pilot-stage, or confined largely to the labs that build them.

claims.claim: The 'prompting is over, now run loops / delegate' narrative is primarily a token-consumption revenue play wrapped in cargo-cult enterprise adoption: when introductory subsidies and free credits end and true per-token costs are charged, enterprise AI usage and the headline internal-productivity figures (such as 'sixty-five percent of code') will not translate into a profitable, sustainable base of enterprise AI demand outside the big labs and their hyperscaler backers.
claims.resolution: Within 12 months, charging true at-cost pricing leaves enterprise AI demand flat or contracting and no profitable, sustainable enterprise AI demand base emerges beyond OpenAI/Anthropic and hyperscalers. Fails if priced-at-cost enterprise AI demand grows on sustainable margins with documented ROI.

claims.claim: Clear, CEO-level accountability for AI is a causal driver of return, not just a correlate: organisations where the CEO personally owns AI strategy will, over time, show genuinely superior, measurable AI outcomes (not merely higher self-reported confidence) versus those with diffuse or no ownership.
claims.resolution: By end 2027, independent or audited evidence (beyond self-report surveys) shows organisations with clear CEO/executive AI ownership achieving materially better measured AI ROI or productivity than comparable firms without it. Fails if the ownership-ROI link remains confined to survey sentiment with no measured outperformance, or disappears under controlled analysis.

claims.claim: Enterprise AI has no measurable ROI: once customers pay true, unsubsidised token costs, the favourable 'reported ROI' figures (such as KPMG's 3x and CEO-ownership uplifts) will not convert into audited, demonstrable net returns, and surveys will keep substituting executive sentiment for arithmetic.
claims.resolution: By mid-2027, no body of audited, priced-at-cost evidence demonstrates positive net enterprise AI ROI at scale; ROI discussion remains dominated by self-report surveys and anecdotes. Fails if credible audited analyses show sustained positive enterprise AI ROI at real prices.

claims.claim: The bot-sitting productivity paradox is a transition artefact, not a ceiling: organisations that do the real work of transformation — governance, training, rewarding AI skills, building human infrastructure — will convert individual AI time savings into measurable organisation-level performance gains, and a rerun of this study in the agentic era would amplify rather than nullify the upside.
claims.resolution: By end-2027, credible evidence (audited outcomes or a repeat large-sample study) shows 'transformative' organisations turning AI use into significant, measured organisation-level gains, and the share of organisations reporting significant improvement rises well above the current 13%. Fails if the org-level gap persists or widens despite transformation efforts.

claims.claim: The roughly trillion-dollar AI/data-centre buildout is cargo-cult spending driven by a lack of other ideas, not by arriving value; it will not generate organisational returns proportionate to the outlay, and the AI 'transformation' narrative will keep substituting ritual and planted stories for demonstrable results.
claims.resolution: By end-2027, the large AI capex shows no proportionate audited return — evidenced by impairments/writedowns, stalled data-centre economics, or continued absence of organisation-level ROI at real cost. Fails if AI investment demonstrably produces returns justifying the spend.

claims.claim: The constraining of frontier models to a small licensed group of partners marks a durable, structural shift: even after Mythos and GPT-5.6 are broadly released, access to top models will remain tiered — nation, then agencies, then chosen firms — producing a measurable intelligence advantage for those at the front of the queue that does not close.
claims.resolution: By end-2027, frontier-model access remains structurally tiered (formal or de facto government-gated early access), AND there is credible evidence that front-of-queue access yields a real capability or economic advantage over those on broadly available models. Fails if frontier access reverts to broad simultaneous public availability with no durable advantage to early-access holders.

claims.claim: The premise that frontier AI access is 'access to the future' is bubble rhetoric: the roughly $1.1 trillion in compute commitments behind these models is not matched by real demand or returns, and the value gap between frontier and cheap/open models will prove economically immaterial rather than world-altering.
claims.resolution: By end-2027, the AI capex shows no proportionate audited return — evidenced by writedowns/impairments, a financing pullback, or the continued absence of frontier-only ROI at real (unsubsidised) cost, while cheaper/open models capture most practical value. Fails if rationed frontier access demonstrably produces returns or advantages justifying the spend.

claims.claim: The AI economy is genuinely revenue-validated and self-sustaining, not merely a promise: Exponential View's audit shows demand backed by realised revenue ($110B banked, a $175B run rate), quarterly revenue already exceeds CapEx depreciation, and older GPUs earn yields well past their six-year life — so the return-on-CapEx indicators are far more positive than the bubble discourse suggests.
claims.resolution: By end-2027, hyperscaler and lab AI economics show durable, unsubsidised returns — audited (GAAP) AI revenue growing faster than AI-related CapEx and depreciation, with no large writedowns or financing pullback. Fails if AI revenue remains reliant on hyperscaler subsidy of their own labs, capex persistently outpaces cashflow, or major impairments appear.

claims.claim: The AI build-out serves demand that does not exist outside OpenAI and Anthropic; hyperscaler CapEx will outpace cashflow from Q3 2026, headline 'run rate' revenue is recycled subsidy rather than real return, and the spend will ultimately surface as writedowns rather than durable economic value.
claims.resolution: By end-2027, evidence of a reckoning: hyperscaler AI CapEx exceeding free cash flow with no proportionate audited return, and/or material writedowns, impairments, or a financing pullback across the AI supply chain (e.g. neoclouds, OpenAI/Anthropic). Fails if AI revenue proves broad-based and self-funding with capex comfortably covered and no significant impairments.

claims.claim: The industry's inference-cost breakthroughs are real and durable: optimisation techniques (e.g. OpenAI's ~50% cut) and shifts to own/open-weight models are structurally lowering the cost of running frontier-class AI without materially degrading quality.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check-by date, at least one major lab or independent benchmark documents a sustained per-task inference cost reduction of 40%+ at comparable quality, and blended token prices for frontier-class output continue to fall rather than rise.

claims.claim: No AI lab is genuinely profitable on inference; cheaper tokens are subsidised customer-acquisition, and the leading labs will keep burning cash with capex and compute obligations outrunning inference revenue.
claims.resolution: Zitron vindicated if no major lab (OpenAI/Anthropic) discloses an audited, unsubsidised positive inference gross margin by the check-by date and reported losses/compute obligations continue to grow; NLW's side favoured if a lab publishes real inference profit.

claims.claim: High-AI-adoption firms hiring more people — including 12% entry-level growth per Ramp/Revelio — reflects genuine complementarity, and the pattern will persist and broaden rather than reverse.
claims.resolution: By the check date, follow-up payroll data (Ramp/Revelio or comparable large-sample studies) still shows high-AI-adoption firms growing headcount faster than low-adoption firms, including at entry level. Fails if the gap closes or reverses, or if the effect is credibly shown to be a spending/selection artefact.

claims.claim: Hyperscaler AI capex will outpace their operating cash flows as of Q3 2026, marking the start of a protracted investment bust.
claims.resolution: By the check date, reported Q3 2026 figures show combined AI capex at Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta exceeding operating cash flow (per Epoch AI's framing Zitron endorses), and at least one hyperscaler guides capex down citing demand. Fails if cash flows keep covering capex and guidance keeps rising.

claims.claim: Open-weight, custom post-trained, and multi-model stacks (e.g. GLM 5.2, Cursor Composer, Harvey+Fireworks) will move from curiosity to standard enterprise practice, with local/open-weight AI becoming a routine boardroom option rather than an edge case.
claims.resolution: By the check date, credible enterprise-adoption surveys or major-vendor disclosures show open-weight/self-hosted or custom post-trained models in mainstream production use at a material share of large firms. Fails if closed frontier APIs remain the near-universal default and open-weight enterprise use stays marginal.

claims.claim: The AI capex boom is a bubble: hyperscaler AI spending will keep outpacing earnings and free cash flow, and disappointing returns will trigger a financing pullback and 'protracted investment bust' rather than an orderly maturation.
claims.resolution: Zitron vindicated if by the check date at least one of the big four hyperscalers guides AI capex down citing weak returns, or a major AI-supply-chain borrower (e.g. Oracle, CoreWeave) hits a debt-servicing crisis. NLW's side favoured if capex keeps rising, cash flows keep covering it, and no such pullback or distress occurs.

claims.claim: AI is making the solo million-dollar company a durable category: solo business formation in high-AI-adoption sectors and the number of solopreneurs reaching $1M revenue will keep growing even as token subsidies end and usage-based pricing spreads.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if follow-up Stripe/Census-style data through the check date show the solo $1M cohort and solo business applications in professional services/info/finance still growing (or holding) after material token repricing. Fails if formation or cohort revenue visibly deflates as subsidised pricing is withdrawn.

claims.claim: AI demand is artificial: end users get $30-40 of compute per dollar paid, and once subsidised pricing ends and market incentives shift, consumer and small-business AI usage and revenue will collapse rather than persist — no bailout will save the sector because it is systemically irrelevant.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date a substantial repricing toward true cost produces a clear contraction in AI usage/subscriptions and small-business AI-driven revenue. Fails if usage and paying demand persist or grow at materially higher effective prices.

claims.claim: Interpretability that reads a model's live 'workspace' (J-Lens) is a practical lever for capability: training the model's silent thoughts (counterfactual reflection training) will translate into measurably better, more honest model behaviour in shipped products, not just lab demos.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, Anthropic (or peers) ship a model whose reliability/honesty gains are credibly attributed to interpretability-guided training such as counterfactual reflection training, evidenced in a model card or peer analysis. Fails if the technique remains a research demonstration with no attributable production improvement.

claims.claim: AI capability progress is stalling and the economics are unsustainable: the sector needs roughly $3 trillion or more in annual revenue by end of 2030 to justify planned data-centre buildouts (estimated $9.5-15 trillion), a sum the debt markets cannot supply, so no interpretability advance changes the trajectory.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date frontier AI revenue remains an order of magnitude short of the multi-trillion trajectory and data-centre financing visibly strains or contracts. Fails if AI revenue scales toward those figures and buildout financing proceeds without systemic distress.

claims.claim: Even if Beijing restricts overseas distribution of Chinese frontier open-weight models, Western alternatives (NVIDIA Nemotron, Google Gemma, Microsoft Frontier Tuning, fine-tuned specialist models, model routers) will fill the gap and keep enterprise per-task AI costs on a downward path.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, enterprise per-task inference costs continue to fall (or hold flat) and Western open-weight/fine-tuning options show mass enterprise adoption, regardless of any Chinese export restriction. Fails if a Chinese cutoff (or its anticipation) produces sustained per-task cost rises or measurable enterprise pullback from agentic AI usage.

claims.claim: NVIDIA's projected $1 trillion in Blackwell/Vera Rubin GPU sales through end-2027 requires roughly $435 billion in annual AI compute demand that does not exist outside subsidised OpenAI/Anthropic spend; the demand will not materialise and the buildout financing will visibly strain.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date NVIDIA materially misses its trillion-dollar sales trajectory, or hits it only alongside visible financing distress (vendor backstops expanding, neocloud defaults, hyperscaler capex cuts). Fails if the sales land and are matched by broad-based, non-circular compute demand from customers beyond OpenAI and Anthropic.

claims.claim: Voice is becoming a primary coordination layer for AI work: full-duplex models like GPT Live will move voice interaction from niche to mainstream, shifting even habitual typers (per Altman) and making orchestrator-plus-implementer multi-model workflows the norm.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, full-duplex voice interfaces are a widely adopted mode of AI use (competing labs ship equivalents, credible usage data shows voice as a substantial and growing share of interactions). Fails if voice remains a demo-and-accessibility niche while text continues to dominate real work.

claims.claim: AI demand is manufactured, not organic: excluding OpenAI and Anthropic, the AI industry earns at best about $20 billion a year, and this will not grow into anything approaching the revenue needed to justify the buildout, because subsidised pricing (selling ~$40 of compute for $1) is the only thing sustaining usage.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date AI industry revenue excluding OpenAI and Anthropic remains an order of magnitude below buildout-justifying levels and visible retrenchment follows any subsidy withdrawal. Fails if ex-OpenAI/Anthropic AI revenue scales several-fold with customers demonstrably paying unsubsidised prices.

claims.claim: The model race has durably moved to cost: frontier-quality intelligence will keep getting cheaper per task (GPT-5.6 at a third of Fable's cost, Muse Spark at a tenth), and these cheap tiers will hold or lower their prices while paid enterprise usage of agentic knowledge-work products (ChatGPT Work) grows.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date advertised per-task/API prices for frontier-class models (GPT-5.6 family, Muse Spark) have held or fallen despite rising memory input costs, and agentic knowledge-work products show growing paid enterprise adoption. Fails if the cheap tiers are repriced upward, quietly rate-limited, or withdrawn, or if enterprise agentic adoption visibly stalls.

claims.claim: AI capex is driving a structural memory crisis: NVIDIA now takes roughly 65% of the world's high-bandwidth memory, the DRAM triopoly (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) is repricing at will, consumer electronics prices will keep rising as long as hyperscaler capex is sustained — and the moment capex slows, the memory industry faces a supply glut and profit collapse worse than any prior cycle.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date DRAM/NAND contract prices remain sharply elevated with continued consumer-device price rises while capex persists, or a hyperscaler capex slowdown triggers visible memory-industry distress (cancellations, inventory gluts, collapsing margins at Micron/SK Hynix/Samsung). Fails if memory prices normalise without a capex pullback and device prices stabilise, or if capex slows and memory makers absorb it without severe distress.

claims.claim: The cheaper GPT-5.6 variants (Terra and Luna) are 'basically better than GLM performance for lower than GLM costs' — frontier labs will fully participate in the cheap-model shift rather than ceding it to open-source challengers.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date independent benchmark aggregators (e.g. Artificial Analysis) show GPT-5.6 Terra/Luna matching or beating GLM 5.2 on overall quality at equal or lower per-token price. Fails if GLM 5.2 (or a successor open model) clearly beats them on quality-per-dollar.

claims.claim: Hyperscalers still won't prove the demand: through the next earnings season, none of Microsoft, Google, Amazon or Meta will break out actual standalone AI revenue figures, because (he argues) the numbers would expose how little real demand exists outside OpenAI and Anthropic's compute spend.
claims.resolution: Fails if by the check date any of the four hyperscalers discloses a clear standalone AI revenue line in its quarterly results. Vindicated if all four continue reporting AI only through blended segments and capex commentary.

claims.claim: The 'software factory' problems that surfaced in coding — runaway cost from over-powered models, security holes from over-permissioned tools, wildly variable human usage — will recur as agents move into non-engineering functions (product, marketing, sales), because what AI engineers argue about today is what every knowledge worker argues about roughly six months later.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date there is documented evidence of enterprises deploying agents in marketing, sales or product hitting the same cluster of cost-control, governance and security problems, and vendors shipping 'factory'-style controls for those functions. Fails if agent adoption outside engineering proceeds without this recognisable pattern, or stalls entirely.

claims.claim: The 'loops' fashion (agents prompting agents, running continuously) is primarily a device to increase token consumption and revenue rather than a genuine productivity advance, and — like other cargo-cult rituals — will deliver no independently verified output gains before the buzzword recedes.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date no credible independent (non-vendor) study shows loop/continuous-agent workflows materially raising developer output, and the 'loops' framing fades as vendors move to the next term. Fails if independent evidence demonstrates loop-based workflows durably raise output per engineer, or the pattern is retained after token subsidies tighten.

claims.claim: Enterprise fine-tuning and open-weights customisation (via platforms like Thinking Machines' Tinker/Inkling and Microsoft Frontier Tuning) is a real emerging category offering cost control and data sovereignty, with genuine 'alpha for nimble teams' who experiment now.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, there is credible non-vendor evidence (enterprise case studies, disclosed adoption or spend, or independent analyst data) that businesses are adopting open-weights fine-tuning platforms at meaningful scale for cost or data-sovereignty reasons, and that early movers captured a measurable advantage. Fails if such platforms see negligible enterprise traction or fine-tuning is broadly abandoned in favour of renting general frontier models.

claims.claim: OpenAI's economics are unsustainable and it will effectively run out of money in 2027 — needing an emergency raise, a down-round, a bailout, or folding into Microsoft — because no amount of enterprise AI spending (open weights or otherwise) produces the returns to justify its ~$850bn planned burn.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date OpenAI has run an emergency or down-round raise on distressed terms, taken a government/hyperscaler bailout, folded into Microsoft, or breached a major compute contract (e.g. Oracle). Fails if OpenAI completes a healthy up-round or IPO and continues operating independently and solvently through 2027.

claims.claim: The trajectory of open Chinese models is now as steep as the closed US frontier: Chinese open-weight models will continue to close (not fall further behind) the gap to the best US closed models, staying within roughly a three-month lag on major public benchmarks.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, the leading Chinese open-weight model remains within about three months of the best US closed-source model on a recognised independent benchmark (e.g. Artificial Analysis intelligence index), and the gap has not widened from its July 2026 level. Fails if the best US closed models pull materially further ahead of the top Chinese open model on those benchmarks.

claims.claim: Serving frontier-class inference (open-weights models like Kimi K3 included) is not profitable, and no provider will demonstrate audited profit from hosting such a model: cheaper Chinese open models undercut the labs' economics without creating a viable, profitable inference business.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date no inference provider or self-hoster has publicly shown audited profit from serving a frontier-class (K3-scale) model, and price competition continues to compress margins. Fails if a provider publishes credible, audited figures showing frontier-class inference served at a durable profit.

claims.claim: The largest gains from Fable 5 / GPT-5.6-class models come not from doing existing work faster but from moving AI onto high-leverage 'impact' work and unlocking categories of work that weren't previously possible; organisations and individuals who merely automate busywork will see far smaller returns than those who raise their ambition.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date credible evidence (independent productivity studies or documented case reports) shows the largest measured value from these models concentrated in high-judgement/'impact' work delegated to AI, rather than in routine automation. Fails if measured value continues to come overwhelmingly from speeding up existing routine tasks, with no clear premium for the 'raise your ambition' approach.

claims.claim: 'Loops' - agents left running to prompt themselves - are a token-burning ploy with no demonstrated productivity benefit; the industry is pushing them to raise revenue, not because they work.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date no credible independent evidence (controlled study or audited case) shows loop-based agentic workflows delivering measurable net productivity gains over single-pass or human-directed prompting, while per-task token consumption rises. Fails if a credible independent study or audited deployment shows loops producing a real, measured productivity improvement that justifies their extra cost.

claims.claim: The de facto informal regime governing model releases will move toward formalisation, and the US will take concrete regulatory action to restrict Chinese open-weight models - shaping which models enterprises can access and at what cost.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date the US has instituted a formal approval/clearinghouse mechanism gating frontier-model release (e.g. Gold Eagle) and/or taken concrete regulatory action against Chinese open-weight models (entity-list additions, an executive order creating hosting liability, or an effective ban). Fails if the regime remains genuinely voluntary with no such formal mechanism or restriction in place.

claims.claim: OpenAI has no meaningful return on investment and remains deeply unprofitable; the premium-frontier business that justifies the industry's trillions in capex does not generate tangible, measurable returns and is a systemic liability.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date OpenAI is still reporting large net losses with no credible path to profitability and no independent evidence of ROI justifying the capex (or a major funding failure / restructuring occurs). Fails if OpenAI demonstrates sustainable profitability or audited positive ROI that justifies the premium-frontier spend.

claims.claim: A next-generation OpenAI model (presumed GPT-6) already demonstrates cyber and reasoning capability far ahead of anything publicly shipped, and GPT-6 is reportedly confirmed for release in early August 2026.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if OpenAI publicly releases a model recognised as GPT-6 by the check date, presenting a clear capability step beyond the currently shipped frontier (e.g. GPT-5.6 Sol / Fable 5). Fails if no such GPT-6 release has occurred by the check date, or the released model shows no material capability jump over what was already shipped.

claims.claim: AI capability progress is decelerating, and dramatic one-off demonstrations do not translate into broad, reliable, economically useful capability: benchmark and demo gains keep costing more while reliability and ROI do not follow.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date there is no credible independent evidence of broad, sustained improvement in frontier-model reliability on ordinary real-world tasks AND leading labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) still lack audited positive ROI on their frontier spend. Fails if independent evidence shows both a measurable, broad reliability improvement on real workloads and a credible path to / demonstration of positive ROI.

claims.claim: The current China-driven selloff is another recurring 'AI freakout' rather than the onset of a real crash: the market's compulsive bubble-hunting acts as a pressure-release valve that keeps a runaway 1999-style AI bubble from forming, so no such broad boom-and-bust collapse takes hold.
claims.resolution: Fails if by the check date there has been a 1999-2000-style AI bubble collapse, i.e. a broad, sustained crash in AI/AI-exposed equities (order of 40%+ peak-to-trough) accompanied by a wave of failures or defaults among major AI infrastructure players. Vindicated if no such systemic AI-equity collapse has occurred and the sector's valuation stress remained a series of contained, recoverable pullbacks.

claims.claim: AI data-centre construction is a debt-funded asset bubble: real compute demand is roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the capacity being built, 70-90% of it comes from OpenAI and Anthropic, and the SPV/off-balance-sheet debt behind data centres will begin to show subprime-style distress.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if by the check date there is credible evidence of data-centre SPV distress (defaults, breached debt-service ratios, cancelled financings tied to unpaid contracts) AND compute demand remains concentrated in OpenAI, Anthropic and their hyperscaler backers with little diverse third-party revenue. Fails if substantial third-party (non-hyperscaler, non-OpenAI/Anthropic) compute revenue materialises at scale and the data-centre debt structures continue to be serviced without notable default or distress.

claims.claim: Following Anthropic economist Peter McCrory, AI will not cause a noticeable rise in US unemployment over the next year, because it is behaving as a skill-biased, labour-augmenting technology that complements expertise rather than replacing headcount; the recent lift in labour productivity (about 2% a year, up from 1.6% pre-pandemic) reflects real AI-driven gains.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, US unemployment remains near full employment (broadly in the 4-5% range) with no credible evidence of a material, AI-attributable rise in joblessness, and labour-productivity growth holds around or above 2%. Fails if unemployment rises materially with credible attribution to AI displacement, or if the productivity uptick reverses toward or below the pre-pandemic 1.6% trend.

claims.claim: The AI build-out is producing no actual return on investment - no revenue, profitability, productivity gains or anything tangible and measurable - and is 'the greatest capital misallocation in history', sustained only because OpenAI (the linchpin, intending to burn over $852bn by 2030) has not yet collapsed.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, there is credible evidence that AI has failed to produce measurable aggregate productivity or profit returns AND OpenAI shows acute financial distress (failed/renegotiated funding, defaulted or unmet remaining performance obligations, or collapse). Fails if OpenAI's committed spending continues to be funded and serviced without acute distress AND independent evidence shows durable AI-attributable productivity or profit gains at scale.

claims.claim: Endorsing Ethan Mollick's refreshed guide, that for intensive agentic work there are effectively only two real choices - ChatGPT or Claude - and that Google has no leading frontier model and nothing comparable to Codex or Claude Code, so Gemini should not be anyone's primary agentic system.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, Google still has no frontier model or agentic coding harness that independent reviewers and mainstream 'which AI should I use' guidance rank alongside ChatGPT and Claude for sustained agentic work. Fails if Gemini (or a Google successor) is by then routinely recommended as a primary agentic system on equal footing, as Mollick himself concedes could happen quickly.

claims.claim: That the popularity of AI 'has come entirely from social pressure and endlessly-discounted access', and that the industry's push toward agentic loops is a token-burn revenue mechanism rather than a demonstrated productivity gain - implying usage falls away once real, unsubsidised prices are charged.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, credible reporting or disclosed figures show paid agentic/AI seats shrinking or renewals falling materially once free credits and discounts are withdrawn, with no independent evidence of measurable output gains from agentic loops. Fails if paid seat counts and renewal rates on full-price agentic tiers hold or grow through price rises, or if credible independent studies show measurable productivity gains from agentic loop workflows.

claims.claim: That most knowledge workers are not model omnivores but locked into a single company's ecosystem, so Claude Opus 5 should be judged as the daily-driver slot in Anthropic's stack rather than as a Fable replacement — and on that reading it is a significant upgrade that will hold that slot.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, credible usage data or enterprise surveys show most AI-using knowledge workers still working predominantly within one vendor's models, AND Opus 5 (or its direct successor) is Anthropic's routinely-used everyday model rather than one users work around. Fails if multi-model routing and cross-lab switching become the normal enterprise pattern, or if Opus 5 is widely abandoned in favour of Opus 4.8, Sonnet or rival models on reliability grounds.

claims.claim: That almost nothing will actually be built at the ten-gigawatt SoftBank-affiliate campus behind NVIDIA's reported $250bn financing guarantee — 'somewhere between nothing and very little' — because the deal is a mechanism for booking GPU sales rather than a response to real demand; at prevailing build rates the site would take over a decade to complete.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, the campus has no more than token construction — no substantial energised critical IT load, or the financing guarantee is never executed, restructured away, or the project is quietly shelved. Fails if the guarantee is signed and a material share of the site is under active construction with meaningful capacity energised and contracted to OpenAI on the announced schedule.

claims.claim: That the open-weight coalition — roughly $8tn of market cap, plus OpenAI added after pushback — is broad enough to defeat the proposed US ban on Chinese open-weight models, with Lutnick's 'compete, don't ban' position prevailing over the Bessent/security camp, leaving Anthropic isolated rather than vindicated.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, no US statute, executive order or Commerce rule broadly prohibits US persons or firms from downloading, hosting or building on Chinese open-weight models, and policy instead targets specific unlawful extraction. Fails if a broad ban or effective equivalent (entity-listing the major Chinese open-model labs, or barring their weights from US distribution) is enacted.

claims.claim: That NVIDIA's investment in Safe Superintelligence is demand manufacture rather than a bet on research — SSI being, in his words, a company with no products or plans other than to rent NVIDIA GPUs — and so will not produce a commercial product or third-party revenue within the window, whatever compute it is given.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, SSI has released no generally available commercial product and reports no meaningful external revenue, while having taken NVIDIA capital and Vera Rubin capacity. Fails if SSI ships a product, licenses its technology, or discloses material third-party revenue by then.

claims.claim: That no thoughtful, coalition-building international pacing effort will actually materialise — US AI policy will continue to be made ad hoc by a handful of officials and the president's mood, so the Pacing the Frontier letter will not produce a real international mechanism, and in particular nothing that includes China, which NLW identifies as the letter's true subtext and the only constituency that would make pacing work.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, no international body, treaty or formal agreement exists with US participation that sets technical or governance mechanisms for pacing frontier AI capability, and no such process includes China as a participant. Fails if such a mechanism is established and China is party to it, or if a US-led multilateral pacing process is formally constituted with Chinese participation.

claims.claim: That the US government will not rescue the frontier AI labs — no bailout, no sovereign wealth fund stake, no CHIPS-style special treatment — because any such package would have to pass Congress and would be politically intolerable; the industry's safety and importance framing is the groundwork for asking, but the ask will fail.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, no federal legislation, executive order or Treasury facility provides equity investment, loan guarantee, debt backstop or comparable financial rescue to OpenAI, Anthropic or their data-centre financing. Fails if any such federal support is enacted or executed, including a sovereign-fund equity swap of the kind Altman has floated.

claims.claim: That enterprise AI adoption is now structurally durable rather than experimental — organisations that blew through annual AI budgets in months will raise those budgets rather than cut back, because AI spend behaves like labour priced in tokens rather than software priced in seats, and the capability gap keeps widening.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, large enterprise AI-spend surveys (KPMG, McKinsey, Bain or equivalent) and hyperscaler AI-segment disclosures show aggregate enterprise AI budgets rising year on year into FY2027 with consumption growing, and consumption or outcome-based pricing displacing per-seat pricing at major vendors. Fails if aggregate enterprise AI budgets are reported flat or falling, or if enforced token caps and pilot cancellations dominate the reporting.

claims.claim: That the unit economics force a repricing upwards — as infrastructure gets more expensive to build and run, hyperscalers and neoclouds will have to charge materially more for compute, and the only two customers large enough to absorb it, OpenAI and Anthropic, cannot pay for it.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, a major hyperscaler or neocloud materially raises compute or inference list prices, or a large AI compute commitment is publicly renegotiated, deferred or written down. Fails if per-unit inference prices at comparable capability continue to fall and OpenAI and Anthropic meet their disclosed compute commitments without renegotiation or new rescue financing.

claims.claim: That the AI drawdown was mechanical rather than fundamental — leverage, forced liquidation and risk-off macro, not any change in belief about AI — and that underlying demand keeps growing, so lab revenue continues to accelerate and the data-centre debt does not break.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, OpenAI and Anthropic revenue run rates are higher than the $50B and $71B cited here, no hyperscaler-linked data-centre financing has defaulted or been restructured, and AI-name equity weakness is attributable to macro rather than to disclosed demand shortfalls. Fails if lab revenue growth stalls or reverses, or if a major data-centre financing defaults, is restructured or requires rescue.

claims.claim: That data-centre special purpose vehicles are the AI bubble's CDOs — poorly underwritten, effectively uncollateralised debt distributed to private credit, insurers and pension schemes — and that only ten or fifteen deal failures are needed to trigger a panic, with most of the money invested in data-centre debt ultimately lost.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, multiple data-centre SPV or neocloud financings have breached coverage covenants, defaulted or been written down, with disclosed losses at private credit funds, insurers or pension schemes, and secondary spreads on data-centre securities remain materially wider than at issuance. Fails if data-centre debt performs to schedule, spreads normalise, and no cluster of SPV or neocloud defaults occurs.

claims.claim: That overspending beats underspending on a one-year view — a company that wildly overspends on AI via an internal usage leaderboard will be materially further ahead than a comparable company that underspends out of fear of proving ROI; and that higher-value work inherently consumes more tokens, so the direction of travel is upward consumption, not restraint.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, published evidence — company disclosures, a controlled study, or comparable-cohort research — shows heavy-AI-usage organisations outperforming AI-rationing peers on output or productivity measures, and enterprise token consumption per user continues to rise. Fails if the leaderboard-era heavy spenders (Meta, Uber, and similar) show no measurable advantage over constrained peers, or if enterprise consumption per user flattens or falls while outcomes hold.

claims.claim: That heavy AI usage is loss-making for the vendor rather than the customer — flat-rate plans let users consume many multiples of what they pay (a $200 plan absorbing $8,000-$14,000 of usage; Copilot subscribers burning over 25 times their fee) — and that this subsidy, not customer discipline, is what makes current AI spend look affordable.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, major flat-rate AI plans are converted to metered or hard-capped billing, effective prices per unit of comparable work rise, or a leading lab discloses negative inference gross margins. Fails if flat-rate heavy-use plans persist at similar effective prices and a leading lab publishes positive, audited inference gross margins.

claims.claim: That the capability overhang is the market opportunity — that models already released can do far more than the systems around them permit, so the bulk of near-term AI value will be created at the applied layer by redesigning workflows, not by the next frontier model; and that verifiable domains (maths, code, cyber) will be automated substantially ahead of unverifiable ones (legal, marketing, sales).
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, application-layer AI companies (not the frontier labs) account for the majority of new third-party AI revenue growth, and measured automation or benchmark progress in verifiable domains clearly outpaces that in unverifiable professional domains. Fails if value continues to concentrate in the labs and infrastructure, or if unverifiable domains show comparable displacement to maths and code.

claims.claim: That the economics get worse as the bubble inflates — infrastructure becomes more expensive to build, so hyperscalers and neoclouds must charge materially more for compute to reach profitability, and the only two customers of sufficient scale (OpenAI and Anthropic) cannot pay it; therefore frontier capability demonstrations such as $200-per-proof results do not reflect sustainable prices.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, published compute or frontier-model list prices for comparable reasoning workloads have risen rather than fallen, or a leading lab discloses negative inference gross margins while renegotiating or defaulting on compute commitments. Fails if the effective price of a comparable frontier reasoning task has fallen materially and a leading lab publishes positive, audited inference gross margins.

claims.claim: That the era of AI washing is ending because enterprise buyers have become too sophisticated to fool — evidenced by the shift from counting first use cases to debating open-weights policies, model routing and cost provisioning — so that PR-driven, cost-cut-framed AI announcements will stop delivering board and market rewards, and organisations treating AI purely as an efficiency play will be outperformed by those redesigning processes and roles around it.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, the share of large-employer job-cut announcements attributing cuts to AI has fallen materially from the 40% of May 2026's 97,000 US cuts, AI-attributed layoff announcements no longer produce positive share-price reactions on average, and enterprise adoption surveys show open-weights policies and model-routing governance as mainstream practice. Fails if AI-attributed cost-cutting announcements continue at or above current rates and continue to be rewarded by markets.

claims.claim: That genuine AI demand outside the frontier labs barely exists — that roughly 55-73% of the big three hyperscalers' AI revenues are OpenAI's and Anthropic's own compute spend (funded substantially by those same hyperscalers), and that embedded AI software has no real pull, evidenced by Microsoft 365 Copilot generating only about $3.9bn in FY2026 across roughly 30 million paid seats.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, a hyperscaler discloses AI revenue net of OpenAI/Anthropic compute spend and that figure is in the low tens of billions or below against reported capex, or if AI-segment growth at Amazon, Microsoft or Google decelerates sharply following any reduction in lab compute commitments. Fails if a hyperscaler breaks out AI revenue showing lab customers below roughly one third of the total, or if Copilot-class embedded AI revenue per paid seat rises materially toward list price.

claims.claim: That the data centre backlash is driven by loss of agency rather than objection to AI, and is therefore fixable by builders: projects that negotiate fully in the open, drop non-disclosure agreements on local councils, cover community electricity cost increases and budget generously for local benefit will win approval, while the 'it's inevitable' and 'China will' arguments will keep failing.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, identifiable data centre projects that ran open negotiations without council NDAs and offered substantial community benefit packages secured local approval at a materially higher rate than comparable NDA-bound projects, and the count of new local moratoriums has stopped rising from the 219 tracked in August 2026. Fails if the moratorium count keeps climbing and transparent, generously compensated projects are rejected at broadly the same rate as secretive ones.

claims.claim: That AI data centre construction is a debt-funded asset bubble: over $500bn of outstanding AI data centre debt, much of it held in special purpose vehicles and variable interest entities kept off hyperscaler balance sheets, is underwritten by compute demand of roughly $100bn a year against the roughly $435bn a year needed to justify planned capacity — so the majority of that debt will go unpaid and much announced capacity will never be built or occupied.
claims.resolution: Vindicated if, by the check date, at least one substantial AI data centre special purpose vehicle has defaulted, been restructured, or had its debt written down, or a hyperscaler or neocloud takes a material impairment on data centre assets, or interconnection queues such as ERCOT's publish withdrawal rates showing the great majority of requested capacity abandoned. Fails if announced capacity converts to energised, revenue-generating data centres at a high rate with no material data centre debt impairments, and non-lab compute revenue grows into the hundreds of billions annually.
